Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Crawl4AI SSRF: crawler process reaching cloud-metadata or RFC1918 internal IPs · [LLM] Crawl4AI /execute_js sandbox escape: crawler/browser process spawning a shell · [LLM] Crawl4AI unauthenticated access to /monitor endpoints (auth bypass)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Crawl4AI /screenshot or /pdf output_path traversal → arbitrary file write outside output dir · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg: Crawl4AI: Multiple Docker API Vulnerabili
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Crawl4AI /screenshot or /pdf output_path traversal → arbitrary file write outside output dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the CWE-22 arbitrary-file-write in Crawl4AI's /screenshot and /pdf endpoints, where an unvalidated output_path lets an attacker drop files outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs. Detects the crawl4ai server process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn) creating files in sensitive locations (cron, .ssh, shell rc files, /etc, /root) it should never write to. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf), the named safe directory (/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs), and the server process identity. A web crawler writing to cron/.ssh/.bashrc is near-zero-FP. Datadog left empty — provided linux.auditd schema lacks a target-file-path field. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI configured with a custom CRAWL4AI_OUTPUT_DIR pointing at /app or /usr/local (operator misconfig)
  • Admin/CI process running inside the container as the same python interpreter doing legitimate package installs into /usr/local
  • Browser engine (chromium) writing cache under /home/appuser/.cache if process attribution rolls up to python
  • Init/entrypoint scripts seeding config into /app on first boot
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/lib/python" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip","setup.py","wheel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full FolderPath/FileName and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the write landed outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs and inspect the dropped file's content (web shell, cron entry, authorized_keys). Correlate with web logs for the /screenshot or /pdf request carrying output_path. 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, kill the crawl4ai worker, and revoke any keys/creds present in the written path; if a cron or authorized_keys entry was added, remove it. 3) Hunt: search all crawl4ai hosts for other writes outside the output dir, and pivot on the source IP across /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js. Upgrade Crawl4AI to >=0.8.7.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn)$"
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI SSRF: crawler process reaching cloud-metadata or RFC1918 internal IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the SSRF chain across Crawl4AI's /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js and webhook endpoints (CWE-918), where attacker-supplied URLs make the server fetch internal services and the 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata endpoint — including the IPv6-mapped bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Flags the crawl4ai/browser process connecting to metadata or private ranges, which a public-web crawler should never do. Rationale: Cloud-metadata IP 169.254.169.254 (and its ::ffff: mapped form, the CVE-2026-53754 bypass) is essentially never a legitimate destination for a public-web crawler, making it a high-fidelity SSRF anchor; RFC1918 hits are the broader hunting tier. Process-scoped to the named crawl4ai runtimes. CloudWatch left empty — IMDS access is host-network, not visible in CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately connecting to an internal Redis (6379) / Postgres (5432) backend on the Docker bridge network
  • Crawl4AI calling a self-hosted LLM/embedding endpoint on a private IP (Ollama, vLLM)
  • Health-check or service-mesh sidecar traffic from the same container to private ranges
  • Crawling an explicitly allowed internal staging site during QA
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort in (6379, 5432, 11434) and not MetadataHit)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination — a hit on 169.254.169.254 is a confirmed SSRF/credential-theft attempt; for RFC1918 hits, check RemotePort/RemoteUrl and whether it matches a known internal service. Pull the matching /crawl, /md, /llm or webhook request from web logs. 2) Contain: if metadata was reached, rotate the instance role / IMDS credentials immediately and enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1); block the source IP and disable /execute_js (CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED). 3) Hunt: review CloudTrail/Activity logs for any API calls made with the instance role shortly after the metadata hit, and pivot on the source IP for internal-range fan-out (port scanning). Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|chromium|chrome|headless_shell|node)$"
| extend MetadataHit = (RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteIP == "::ffff:169.254.169.254")
| where MetadataHit or ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "169.254.0.0/16")
| extend Severity = iff(MetadataHit, "CRITICAL-cloud-metadata", "internal-SSRF")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Severity
| order by Severity asc, Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstIpAddr == "::ffff:169.254.169.254" or ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8000, 8080) or NetworkApplicationProtocol has_any ("http","https")
| extend Severity = iff(DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstIpAddr == "::ffff:169.254.169.254", "CRITICAL-cloud-metadata", "internal-SSRF")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Severity
| order by Severity asc, TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI /execute_js sandbox escape: crawler/browser process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts the arbitrary-JavaScript-execution / hook-sandbox-escape vulnerability (CWE-94) in Crawl4AI's /execute_js endpoint, where attacker JS (or the asyncio/hook bypass) breaks out to OS command execution. Detects the python/uvicorn/gunicorn server or its headless-chromium/node children spawning an interactive shell — behaviour a web crawler never exhibits. Rationale: Process-tree pivot on the article's named runtime (python/uvicorn/gunicorn + the playwright headless-chromium it drives) spawning a shell directly maps the /execute_js RCE and hook sandbox-escape outcome. Datadog left empty — the provided linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent→child constraint cannot be expressed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately shelling out to a PDF/image post-processing tool (wkhtmltopdf, ghostscript) via subprocess
  • Container entrypoint or healthcheck script invoking sh from the gunicorn master
  • Operator running 'docker exec ... bash' attributed to the server process tree
  • A debugging hook intentionally enabled in non-prod that runs shell commands
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","ghostscript","/usr/bin/gs","libreoffice") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — benign post-processing (ghostscript/wkhtmltopdf) vs reverse shell / curl|sh / recon (id, uname, whoami). Correlate timing with a POST to /execute_js in web logs. 2) Contain: kill the shell and parent worker, isolate the container, and disable /execute_js via CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false (and remove --disable-web-security if present). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to UC2 (SSRF egress) and UC1 (file writes), and search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound C2 from the shell PID. Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ash)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI unauthenticated access to /monitor endpoints (auth bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CWE-306 missing-authentication flaw where Crawl4AI's monitor router was mounted without token_dep, exposing destructive endpoints like /monitor/actions/cleanup and the /monitor/ws WebSocket with no auth. Detects successful requests to /monitor paths that carry no Authorization header. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable paths (/monitor/actions/cleanup, /monitor/ws) plus the auth-bypass signature — a successful response with an empty Authorization header. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this needs HTTP request-header visibility that only the reverse-proxy/WAF (Sentinel ImWebSession / CIM Web) carries; Sigma skipped because 'webserver' is outside the allowed logsource categories. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal monitoring/uptime check polling /monitor without a token (pre-patch, by design)
  • An ops dashboard reverse-proxy that strips the Authorization header before the app tier (header invisible to upstream logger)
  • Health probes from Kubernetes/Docker hitting /monitor/* and returning 200
  • Internal load-balancer keep-alive traffic to the monitor WebSocket
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog","Pingdom"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the request reached a destructive endpoint (/monitor/actions/cleanup) vs read-only monitor views, and whether the source IP is internal/expected. Check for a burst of /monitor/* enumeration from one IP. 2) Contain: put the monitor router behind auth (deploy >=0.8.7 / set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN) and restrict network access to the Docker API; block the offending source IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP, pivot to /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js and /crawl activity (UC1/UC2/UC3/UC5) and review whether cleanup actually deleted job/output data.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/monitor/"
| where Url has_any ("/monitor/actions/cleanup","/monitor/actions","/monitor/ws","/monitor/")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","101","204")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/monitor/actions/cleanup*","*/monitor/actions*","*/monitor/ws*","*/monitor/*")) AND Web.status IN ("200","101","204") by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/monitor/actions/cleanup*","*/monitor/actions*","*/monitor/ws*","*/monitor/*")) AND Web.status IN ("200","101","204") by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Crawl4AI web-payload abuse: path traversal, XSS, file:// and metadata-IP in crawl requests AIDelivery Medium
Hunts malicious payloads sent to Crawl4AI's exposed endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf, /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js, /markdown_extraction, /llm_extraction): output_path traversal sequences, stored-XSS markup (CWE-79), file:// LFI URLs, and literal cloud-metadata / IPv6-mapped targets used for SSRF. A single web-log pivot that surfaces exploitation attempts before they succeed. Rationale: Combines the article's full endpoint inventory with concrete exploit signatures it names: output_path traversal, XSS markup, the file:// LFI vector (VulnCheck-confirmed) and the ::ffff: IPv6-mapped metadata bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Hunting tier because many payloads ride in POST bodies that not all proxies log into the URL field — pairs with the behavioural UCs (1/2/3) for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate crawl target whose URL genuinely contains '../' in its query string or path
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Burp, Nuclei) probing the endpoints during authorized testing
  • A crawled page URL that legitimately references file:// in a parameter value
  • Crawling a security blog whose URL contains '<script' or 'onerror=' as article-content text
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nuclei","Burp","sqlmap","Nessus") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: classify the payload type (traversal vs XSS vs file:// vs metadata-IP) and check the HTTP status — a 200 on /screenshot+output_path traversal or /crawl+file:// suggests success. Cross-reference the source IP with UC1/UC2/UC3 host telemetry for an actual file write, SSRF egress, or shell. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, disable /execute_js, and ensure the patched SSRF/path validators are deployed (>=0.8.7). 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct payload that IP sent across all endpoints, and confirm whether any stored XSS persisted in the monitor dashboard (escapeHtml present?).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/screenshot","/pdf","/crawl","/md","/llm","/execute_js","/markdown_extraction","/llm_extraction")
| where Url has_any ("../","..%2f","..%2F","%2e%2e","<script","onerror=","onclick=","onload=","file://","169.254.169.254","::ffff:","metadata.google.internal","output_path=")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Crawl4AI CVE-2026-53753 sandbox-escape payload (gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins) in POST /crawl body AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of the Crawl4AI Docker API AST sandbox escape by matching the frame-introspection chain (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins, __import__) inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy computed-field expression POSTed to /crawl. These Python generator/frame attribute names have zero benign reason to appear in crawl-extraction schemas, making them a high-fidelity exploit signature. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim exploit primitives gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins/__import__ plus the JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema key and the /crawl endpoint. The frame-attribute chain is the literal sandbox-escape technique named by the advisory and has no benign occurrence in extraction schemas. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory Database (CVSS 9.8, fixed 0.8.7) which confirms the gi_frame.f_back computed-field eval() escape. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Nuclei, Burp) replaying the public PoC against an internal Crawl4AI instance during authorised testing
  • Internal red-team validation of the patch on a staging Crawl4AI container
  • A developer pasting the advisory PoC into a request while reproducing the bug for the 0.8.7 upgrade
  • WAF that mirrors blocked-request bodies into the same log index (action=blocked rows — still worth reviewing but not a live compromise)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","reset")  // keep only requests that actually reached the app; drop WAF-blocked replays during triage tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the SourceIP+RequestClientApplication; confirm the body carries a gi_frame/f_back chain inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema, and check the running Crawl4AI version (<=0.8.6 vulnerable) and whether CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN/JWT auth is set. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, remove the container from public network exposure, and rotate any secrets the container can reach (env vars, mounted files, instance role). 3) Hunt: on the affected host run the post-RCE process-tree and credential-enumeration detections from first-seen time, and review egress from the uvicorn/python process to attacker infrastructure.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/crawl"
| where Message has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","JsonCssExtractionStrategy","__import__")
   or RequestContext has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","__import__")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
(sourcetype="*nginx*" OR sourcetype="*apache*" OR sourcetype="*waf*" OR sourcetype="*proxy*") "/crawl" ("gi_frame" OR "f_back" OR "f_builtins" OR "JsonCssExtractionStrategy" OR "__import__")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host, source, sourcetype, clientip
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Crawl4AI/uvicorn post-RCE: Python web service spawning shell or recon binaries AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-53753: the Crawl4AI Python/uvicorn/gunicorn process spawning interactive shells (sh, bash, dash) or reconnaissance utilities (curl, wget, nc, socat, whoami, id, uname). A crawler web service has no legitimate reason to fork these, so this is a high-confidence signal that the AST sandbox escape achieved code execution. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated impact ('execute arbitrary system commands') by pivoting on the exact server stack named in the advisory (Crawl4AI Docker API served by uvicorn/Python) spawning shells or recon tools — a tree that never occurs in normal crawler operation. The pip/pytest/playwright exclusion strips the only routine python-spawns-shell cases. Corroborated via GitLab GLAD entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container build/CI steps where python runs 'pip install' which forks sh (covered by the filter)
  • Crawl4AI/Playwright bootstrapping that shells out to install browser dependencies on first run
  • A devops entrypoint script that uses python to wrap curl/wget for healthchecks
  • Operator debugging the container interactively via 'docker exec' producing python->bash (verify it was a human shell, not the web worker)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install","conda")) and AccountName !in~ ("root")  // optionally drop root-context build steps if the service runs as a non-root crawl user
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the parent uvicorn/python tree; confirm this is the Crawl4AI web worker (not a CI/pip/playwright bootstrap or an interactive docker exec). 2) Contain: isolate the container/host from the network, kill the offending process tree, and snapshot the container filesystem and memory for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to the /crawl WAF detection to find the originating exploit request, and to the credential-enumeration detection to see whether secrets or the metadata endpoint were touched; review all egress from the worker process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI post-RCE credential & cloud-metadata enumeration via Python-spawned subprocess AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts post-exploitation credential theft following CVE-2026-53753: a Crawl4AI Python/shell process reading /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, the process environment (/proc/self/environ, printenv), or the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254). The advisory explicitly calls out 'exfiltrate secrets', and a web crawler reaching these paths is a strong indicator the sandbox escape was used to harvest credentials. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's 'read/write files, and exfiltrate secrets' impact statement and the listed T1552.001 technique. Anchors the well-known secret targets (/etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, IMDS 169.254.169.254) to the Crawl4AI Python/shell parent chain so it fires on attacker harvesting rather than routine admin reads. Corroborated via the GitLab Advisory Database entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1083 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A container entrypoint/healthcheck script reading /etc/passwd to resolve a uid before dropping privileges
  • Legitimate app code calling printenv/env for config diagnostics under the python worker
  • Monitoring agents (Datadog/aws-otel) querying 169.254.169.254 for instance identity — verify the parent is the agent, not the crawl worker
  • An operator running 'cat /etc/passwd' via docker exec while troubleshooting (interactive, not web-worker-spawned)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("datadog-agent","aws-otel-collector","cloud-init")) and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("getent passwd","id -u"))  // drop monitoring agents and benign uid lookups while keeping shadow/environ/IMDS reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which secret was touched (/etc/shadow vs environ vs IMDS) and confirm the parent chain traces to the Crawl4AI uvicorn/python worker rather than a sidecar/monitoring agent; check whether 169.254.169.254 actually returned IAM/role credentials. 2) Contain: rotate every credential reachable from the container — env-var secrets, mounted files, and any cloud instance-profile/role credentials — and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: in CloudTrail, search for AssumeRole and API activity using the container's instance-profile role from new source IPs since first-seen, and pivot to the /crawl exploit and shell-spawn detections to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or FileName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or TargetProcessName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host making an outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 39.107.60.51 used by 15 trojanized JetBrains Marketplace plugins (DeepSeek/CodeGPT clones) to ship stolen OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys. The connection is initiated by the JetBrains IDE JVM the instant a user clicks Apply on the plugin settings, so the process context is a Java/JetBrains runtime, not a browser. Rationale: Anchored on the single hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 (verbatim from the article's network-call code block, defanged 39.107.60[.]51) — a dedicated attacker host with no legitimate use, cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News. Any connection is dispositive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-ai.html • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/sandbox detonating one of the named plugins to reproduce the IOC
  • Threat-intel or attack-surface scanners (Shodan/Censys) probing the IP from a corporate egress
  • IP reuse: the Alibaba Cloud address later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • A SOAR/enrichment playbook auto-resolving or pinging the IOC and generating an event
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is a JetBrains runtime (idea64.exe/pycharm64.exe/java/jetbrains-runtime) and pull the user; enumerate that user's installed JetBrains plugins against the 15 named IDs. 2) Contain: treat every AI provider API key (OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow) entered on that host as compromised — revoke and rotate immediately, uninstall the plugin, and block 39.107.60.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for the IP, and pivot to UC 'malicious JetBrains plugin install' to find dormant infections that haven't yet phoned home.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName,
          SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL,
          ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the application-layer signature of the theft in web-proxy/network-sensor telemetry: a plaintext HTTP POST to the URI path /api/software/<name> carrying the victim's API key as JSON. This survives C2 IP rotation by keying on the distinctive hardcoded URL path, and catches IDE traffic that egresses through a proxy where EDR socket attribution is weak. Rationale: Uses two verbatim article strings — the URL path /api/software/ from the network-call code block and the C2 IP 39.107.60.51 — over plaintext HTTP (article: 'reached over plain HTTP'). The path keys the detection independently of the IP. Datadog/Falcon left empty: standard FDR network events and the listed Datadog sources don't carry HTTP URI paths, so this needs proxy/web-gateway telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fifteen-jetbrains-marketplace/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal/SaaS API that legitimately exposes a '/api/software/' inventory endpoint reached over HTTP
  • Software-asset-management or patch agents POSTing to a vendor '/api/software/' path
  • Web-app vulnerability scanners fuzzing '/api/' routes from a corporate host
  • Proxy replay/cached events double-counting the same flow
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51" or Url has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full request — confirm the host header/destination resolves to 39.107.60.51 and, if PCAP/full-proxy is available, look for the static header X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing an 'sk-' key. 2) Contain: rotate/revoke the leaked provider key(s), remove the offending JetBrains plugin, and add both the IP and the URI path as egress-block + proxy-deny rules. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for any other host hitting /api/software/ (catches infections after a C2 IP change) and correlate with the endpoint-egress UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/software/" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (Url has "/api/software/" or DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51")
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts on-disk presence or install of any of the 15 trojanized JetBrains plugins by matching their Marketplace display names under a JetBrains \plugins\ directory. Covers the initial-access/supply-chain step and surfaces dormant infections on hosts that haven't yet entered an API key or phoned home to the C2. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim list of 15 malicious plugin display names installed under JetBrains \plugins\ paths — the supply-chain delivery artifact. Hunting-tier because the 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone name overlaps the legitimate CodeGPT plugin, so matches need confirmation (pair with the C2-egress UC). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/ • https://hackread.com/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-deepseek-openai-api-keys/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The legitimate 'CodeGPT' plugin (genuine vendor) whose folder name substring overlaps the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone
  • Developers who installed an affected plugin before JetBrains' takedown and have since updated/removed it (stale on-disk artifact)
  • Security team deliberately installing a sample for analysis in a lab VM
  • JetBrains Marketplace cache/temp extraction folders retaining the plugin name after backend disable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Marketplace\\cache\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact plugin ID inside the matched folder's plugin.xml against the 15 known IDs (e.g. org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit) — this disambiguates the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' from the legitimate CodeGPT. 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin, and immediately revoke/rotate any OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key the developer may have entered (assume compromised even without observed egress). 3) Hunt: pivot every matched host to the C2-egress and HTTP-path UCs for 39.107.60.51 to confirm exfiltration, and query software inventory across the fleet for the remaining plugin IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20)
          by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

references:

Critical

Google Vertex AI SDK Flaw Let Attackers Hijack Model Uploads via Bucket Squatting

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 9 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A flaw in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python let an attacker with no access to a victim's project hijack the victim's machine learning model upload and run code inside Google's serving infrastructure. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which found and reported the bug through Google's bug bounty program, calls the technique "Pickle in the Middle" and said it saw no exploitation in the wild.

CVEsCVE-2026-2473
ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Creation of GCS bucket matching predictable Vertex AI staging naming convention · [LLM] Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK (<1.148.0) install detected in pipeline/build
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI model registered with artifact URI in untrusted predictable staging bucket · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vertex AI model registered with artifact URI in untrusted predictable staging bucket AIDelivery Medium
Hunts Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel/UpdateModel audit events whose model artifact lives in a GCS bucket matching the SDK's predictable 'project-vertex-staging-region' naming convention. In the 'Pickle in the Middle' attack the victim SDK silently stages the model in an attacker-squatted bucket of that exact form, so a model whose source URI references a vertex-staging bucket not owned by the project is a direct indicator of upload hijack / model poisoning. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact predictable bucket form 'project-vertex-staging-region' (corroborated verbatim by Unit 42 and CSO Online) and the Vertex AI UploadModel control-plane call. The artifact URI is the one part of the cross-tenant hijack that is logged in the victim's own project (aiplatform.googleapis.com), making it the only victim-side detectable artifact. Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: Vertex AI model-registry audit events are GCP-native and do not land in Defender XDR, the provided Sentinel standard tables, Falcon FDR, or CloudWatch. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wh2j-26j7-9728
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1565.001 T1537
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teams that explicitly set staging_bucket to a shared bucket they legitimately own that happens to contain 'vertex-staging'
  • Central-ML-project architectures where models are intentionally staged cross-project
  • Patched SDK 1.148+ auto-created staging buckets carrying a uuid4 suffix (e.g. vertex-staging-<uuid>)
  • Third-party MLOps platforms registering models from their own managed GCS buckets
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(coalesce(object_path,command), "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}")  // drop patched-SDK uuid4-suffixed buckets
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the UploadModel event, extract the artifact bucket name and run `gsutil ls -L -b gs://<bucket>` / check Resource Manager to confirm which project OWNS that bucket; if the owning project is outside your org, treat as confirmed hijack. 2) Contain: undeploy/delete the affected Model and any Endpoints serving it, rotate the Vertex AI service-agent credentials, and revoke OAuth tokens issued to the serving container; block the foreign bucket. 3) Hunt: review all Models registered since the SDK was last unpatched (<1.148.0) for vertex-staging artifact URIs, and check serving-container egress for metadata-server token theft.
title: Vertex AI Model Upload Referencing Predictable Staging Bucket
id: 7b3e9f42-1c2a-4d8e-9a6b-2f1c3d4e5a6b
description: Detects Vertex AI model upload/update audit events whose artifact references a GCS bucket using the SDK's predictable project-vertex-staging-region naming, an indicator of the Pickle in the Middle bucket-squatting hijack.
references:
    - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
    - attack.t1195.002
    - attack.t1565.001
    - attack.t1537

            - 'ModelService.UploadModel'
            - 'ModelService.UpdateModel'
    keywords:

    condition: selection and keywords
falsepositives:
    - Teams intentionally staging models in a shared cross-project bucket they own
level: medium
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:(google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel OR google.cloud.aiplatform.v1beta1.ModelService.UploadModel OR google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UpdateModel) *vertex-staging*
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Change.object) as object values(Change.object_path) as object_path from datamodel=Change where Change.vendor_product="Google Cloud Platform" Change.action=created (Change.command="*ModelService.UploadModel*" OR Change.command="*ModelService.UpdateModel*" OR Change.object="*aiplatform*model*") by Change.user Change.src Change.command | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | search object_path="gs://*vertex-staging*" OR command="*vertex-staging*" | where NOT match(coalesce(object_path,command), "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}") | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Change.object) as object values(Change.object_path) as object_path from datamodel=Change where Change.vendor_product="Google Cloud Platform" Change.action=created (Change.command="*ModelService.UploadModel*" OR Change.command="*ModelService.UpdateModel*" OR Change.object="*aiplatform*model*") by Change.user Change.src Change.command | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | search object_path="gs://*vertex-staging*" OR command="*vertex-staging*" | where NOT match(coalesce(object_path,command), "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}") | sort - lastTime
Creation of GCS bucket matching predictable Vertex AI staging naming convention AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts storage.buckets.create audit events for buckets matching the Vertex AI SDK's predictable 'project-vertex-staging-region' pattern without the post-patch uuid4 suffix. Defensively this surfaces internal/compromised accounts pre-creating squattable buckets and inventories predictable-name buckets in your own org that are hijack targets for the Pickle in the Middle technique. Rationale: Uses the article's literal predictable bucket form 'project-vertex-staging-region' as the match string and the GCS control-plane storage.buckets.create event. Because the attacker's bucket is created in the attacker's project (not visible to the victim), this is explicitly framed as org-internal hygiene / insider-squatting detection — high FP for orgs still on the pre-1.148 SDK whose legitimate clients auto-create the same name. Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: GCS admin-activity audit logs are GCP-native and absent from those platforms' provided schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1583.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pre-1.148 Vertex AI SDK legitimately auto-creating the default staging bucket for a fresh project+region (expected, high volume)
  • Data scientists manually creating staging buckets following the documented convention
  • Terraform / Deployment Manager IaC provisioning Vertex staging buckets
  • Patched 1.148+ SDK creating uuid4-suffixed vertex-staging buckets (filtered below)
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(object, "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}") AND NOT match(user, "service-.*@gcp-sa-aiplatform\.iam\.gserviceaccount\.com")  // drop uuid4-suffixed patched buckets and the Vertex service agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the creating principal (principalEmail) and project; confirm whether the bucket name lacks a uuid4 suffix (=created by vulnerable SDK or by hand) and whether the creator is a human/CI account vs the gcp-sa-aiplatform service agent. 2) Contain: if created by an unexpected/foreign or recently-compromised principal, lock the bucket, and force-set an explicit org-owned staging_bucket in affected pipelines so the SDK stops resolving predictable names. 3) Hunt: enumerate all vertex-staging buckets across the org, verify ownership, and upgrade every google-cloud-aiplatform install to >=1.148.0 (see SDK-version UC).

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK (<1.148.0) install detected in pipeline/build AIWeaponization High
Alerts on process-creation events showing installation of google-cloud-aiplatform pinned to a version below the patched 1.148.0 release (covers the article's tested-vulnerable 1.139.0/1.140.0 and the pre-fix 1.13x-1.147 range, plus the related CVE-2026-2473 <1.133.0). These versions resolve staging buckets by predictable name without ownership verification, exposing model uploads to bucket-squatting hijack. Rationale: Anchored on the exact patched/vulnerable version boundary the article and Google's advisory state: 1.139.0/1.140.0 tested-vulnerable, full fix in 1.148.0. The regex/version list deliberately matches 1.13x and 1.140-1.147 only, so patched 1.148+ does NOT fire — eliminating the biggest FP source. CloudWatch left empty (endpoint/CI telemetry, not AWS CloudTrail); the version range also covers the corroborated CVE-2026-2473 (<1.133.0) Experiments variant. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wh2j-26j7-9728 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally pinning an old SDK in a sandbox that never calls Model.upload()
  • Requirements-file installs (pip install -r) where the version is in the file, not the command line (detection gap, not a true FP)
  • Mirror/cache warming jobs that pre-download multiple historical versions
  • Reproducible-research environments deliberately frozen to an older version with an explicit org-owned staging_bucket already set
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/CI runner and whether the install feeds a pipeline that calls Model.upload() without an explicit staging_bucket; check whether google-cloud-aiplatform is actually the resolved runtime version (pip show). 2) Contain: upgrade to >=1.148.0 in the affected requirements/lockfile and rebuild the image; set an explicit org-owned staging_bucket in all upload code paths. 3) Hunt: sweep notebooks, CI jobs, and container layers org-wide for the same pinned versions, then pivot to the model-upload-URI and bucket-creation UCs to confirm no hijack already occurred while unpatched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("google-cloud-aiplatform==1.13","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.140","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.141","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.142","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.143","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.144","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.145","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.146","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.147")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("google-cloud-aiplatform==1.13","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.140","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.141","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.142","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.143","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.144","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.145","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.146","google-cloud-aiplatform==1.147")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05

description: |

references:

author: Clankerusecase

detection:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Critical

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 19 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for
